o: We must count **distinct** substrings `t` of `text` such that `t = a + a` for some string `a`. Every echo substring has even length, so for each start index `i` we only try half-lengths `L` with `i + 2L <= n`, and check whether `text[i..i+L)` equals `text[i+L..i+2L)`. In example 1 (`"abcabcabc"`), the matches are `abcabc` (i=0), `bcabca` (i=1), `cabcab` (i=2) — three distinct strings. In example 2, only `ee` and `leetcodeleetcode` qualify. With `n <= 2000`, an $O(n^2)$ algorithm performs about 2 million checks — easily fast enough — while a naive $O(n^3)$ substring-comparison solution is borderline, motivating hashing.
k: An echo substring has even length 2L, so for each start i you only need to test half-lengths L up to (n-i)/2.
Rolling hashes let you compare two substrings of length L in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing, turning the whole search into O(n^2).
Deduplicate by storing (half-length, hash) pairs in a set rather than materializing substrings.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force with a Set of Substrings
a.i: Directly enumerate every start `i` and every feasible half-length `L`; slice out both halves and compare them as raw strings. If they match, insert the full echo substring into a set, which handles distinctness automatically. This is the most literal translation of the problem statement and is correct, but slicing/comparing costs O(L) per check, giving O(n^3) time overall — acceptable conceptually, risky at n = 2000 in slower languages.
s: Initialize an empty set `seen` of strings.
For each start i from 0 to n-1:
For each L from 1 while i + 2L <= n:
If text[i:i+L] == text[i+L:i+2L], add text[i:i+2L] to `seen`.
a.t: O(n^3) time — there are O(n^2) (i, L) pairs and each comparison/slice costs O(L).
a.sp: O(n^3) worst case — the set can hold O(n^2) strings of average length O(n); typically much less.

a.i: Precompute prefix hashes so any substring's hash is obtained in O(1). Then for every start `i` and half-length `L`, compare hash(text[i..i+L)) with hash(text[i+L..i+2L)) in constant time. Deduplicate echoes by inserting `(hash_of_full_substring, L)` into a set — the half-length disambiguates different-length strings sharing a hash value. This yields O(n^2) time with O(n) extra space beyond the set, comfortably fitting the constraints. Using a large random-ish modulus makes collision probability negligible.
s: Build prefix hash array h and power array p with base B and a large modulus M.
Define get(i, j) = (h[j] - h[i] * p[j-i]) mod M for the hash of text[i..j).
For each start i, for each L with i + 2L <= n:
If get(i, i+L) == get(i+L, i+2L), add (get(i, i+2L), L) to a result set.
Return the size of the result set.
a.t: O(n^2) time — O(n) preprocessing plus O(n^2) constant-time hash comparisons.
a.sp: O(n) auxiliary space for the hash/power arrays, plus the result set holding at most O(n^2) entries.

w: In an interview, lead with the brute force to establish correctness, then upgrade to rolling hashes — interviewers expect the $O(n^2)$ solution given $n \le 2000$. Pitfalls: forgetting that only even lengths qualify, off-by-one errors in the half-length bound `(n - i) // 2`, integer overflow in hash arithmetic (use 128-bit math in C++, BigInt in JavaScript, or a modulus below 2^31 with double hashing in Java), and deduplicating by hash alone without encoding the length. Edge cases: single-character input returns 0; highly periodic strings like `"aaaa"` must be counted once per distinct string, not per occurrence. Follow-ups: solve for n up to 10^5 (requires suffix arrays/Z-functions to find, for each split L, positions where the two halves match, then count distinct echoes via LCP reasoning), or handle streaming input.
